analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to wages above $250,000.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2011 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, wages above roughly $107,000 (the 2011 Social Security taxable maximum) are exempt from Social Security payroll taxes, so a dollar earned above that line is taxed less for Social Security than a dollar earned below it. This bill would have kept the tax on wages up to the existing cap and added it back on all wages above $250,000, for employees and the self-employed alike, starting in 2012. The added revenue would flow into Social Security, shoring up a program that pays benefits to retirees, survivors, and disabled workers.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, Social Security would have gained a new, ongoing revenue stream from the highest earners, strengthening the program's finances for current and future retirees, survivors, and disability beneficiaries. Workers and small employers whose wages fall entirely below the $250,000 line would pay nothing new.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the tax code so that Social Security employment and self-employment taxes apply both to remuneration up to the contribution and benefit base and to remuneration in excess of $250,000.
The new tax would have taken effect on remuneration paid after December 31, 2011, for both employees and self-employed earners.
People earning below the $250,000 line pay no additional tax under the bill; the tax applies only to wages and self-employment earnings above that threshold.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on high earners: employees, and people with self-employment income, whose wages or earnings exceed $250,000 in a year would pay Social Security payroll tax on the amount above that line, and their employers would owe the employer share on that portion as well.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves a gap between the current taxable maximum (about $107,000 in 2011) and $250,000 untouched, so a high earner's income in that middle band would still pay no Social Security tax — a design critics called a 'donut hole' that softens the burden on the very top.

Because the employer share of the new tax applies to wages above $250,000, businesses with very highly paid executives would face a new payroll cost on those wages, a cost some would argue comes on top of an economy still recovering from the 2008-2009 recession.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest in design: extending payroll tax above $250,000 would materially improve Social Security's long-term finances without touching benefits or the taxes of roughly 99 percent of earners. The donut-hole gap between the current cap and $250,000 is the main honest criticism, and it makes the bill less comprehensive than proposals to tax all wages above the current cap. The costs fall entirely on the top sliver of earners and their employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2011, and the committee never acted on it — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on September 14, 2011, joined by ten Democratic cosponsors, all senators.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, which was the last action recorded for it in the 112th Congress.
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose wages exceed $250,000 a year are better off, since the additional Social Security tax on their income never took effect. The Finance Committee's inaction also meant the broader 2011-2012 debate over Social Security's finances proceeded without any vote on raising the payroll tax cap.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to apply Social Security payroll taxes to earnings above $250,000.

for.name: 10 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors (Boxer, Whitehouse, Akaka, Leahy, McCaskill, Franken, Blumenthal, Mikulski, and others)

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; Chair Max Baucus (D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All eleven sponsors — one Independent and ten Democrats — caucus with the Democrats, and no Republican cosponsored; the bill never advanced far enough to produce a roll-call.

industries.note: The bill's entire cost falls on earnings above $250,000 a year, which only the top few percent of earners receive. Their interest in avoiding the new tax ran against the program's interest in more revenue.
Retirees, survivors, and disability beneficiaries would have gained from the additional revenue flowing into Social Security, which helps keep scheduled benefits payable.
